note: THE PARAGRAPHPLAN JUDGE'S AXES (kogaki#1533, owner decision 2026-10-23): one responsibility and one sentence per axis, rendered in this order into `paragraph_plan_judge_unit` by its `{{axes}}` token (src/workflow/judge.mjs).

Each axis carries `fixtures`: at least one `defect` record that violates this axis and no other, and one `clean` record, each naming a record under `records`. A record is a judge input whole, or `from` another record with one `edit`: a Paragraph Waypoint replaced (`waypoint`, `paragraph_waypoint`, `to`) a `join` replaced (`waypoint`, `join`), or a Leg Waypoint's `discharges` replaced (`waypoint`, `discharges`), with `owes` setting the Brief rows the Leg owes beside it. `at_waypoint` names the Leg Waypoint a defect sits on.

THE RETENTION RULE: an axis is kept where, over at least `retention.draws_min` draws of `node src/proof-sheet/judge-bench.mjs --axis <id>`, its defect records are refused in at least `defect_refused_with_min` of the draws with the axis and in at most `defect_refused_without_max` without it, and its clean record passes in at least `clean_passed_with_min` with it; an axis failing the rule is removed. Rates are fractions of the draws.

`justified_by` records the bench run that kept the axis: its date, its run directory and its rates. `judge-bench.mjs --record` writes it, or removes the axis that fails the rule; checks/check-paragraph-plan-axes.sh refuses an axis without it.
Countable rules are not axes: the Paragraph Waypoint count against the bound Move's Segments and the one-of `performs` and `point` are refusals of the plan-record validator (src/paragraph-plan.mjs).

segments.operation: opens by asserting one general principle about the motive of a whole class of actors
segments.manner: a brief direct statement, given with no support and no hedging

segments.operation: explains a widely observed and seemingly contradictory self-description by treating it as literally true
segments.relation: it takes the case that looks most like a refutation and turns it into the strongest evidence for the step before
segments.manner: a short quoted self-description stands in for the whole behaviour being explained

segments.operation: shifts the vantage point from an actor's own intention to how the same conduct is received by another party, stated as a general tendency
segments.relation: it keeps the general register of the step before but moves to the other side of the same conduct

segments.operation: labels one present-day instance as a typical case while withholding its detail
segments.relation: it drops from the general tendency to a single instance the reader already knows of

segments.operation: spells out a single instance from both sides in one step, so that two parties acting on the same motive are seen to produce an escalation neither intends
segments.relation: it fills in the instance the step before only labelled, supplying the two halves that make it typical

breaks: hedge the opening principle with qualifications — the explanation that follows has nothing flat enough to lean on, and the reader takes it as one view among several
drop the hardest-looking case and go straight from the principle to the general tendency — the principle reads as naive, and the reader keeps the blame-based explanation they came with
report the quoted self-description as a summary instead — it loses its ring of familiarity and reads as the writer's characterisation rather than something the reader has heard
name the present instance but stop before filling in both sides — the reader is left with a label and never sees two parties acting on the same motive producing the outcome neither chose
insert a stretch of historical background between the general tendency and the present instance — the pairing loses its immediacy and the live case reads as illustration rather than as the point

paragraph_waypoints.point: A state is by nature interested in protecting itself.
The standing declaration that a war being started is a war of defence is literally true of a state's motive.
Any state fears a neighbour's rapid build-up.
The present relation between China and Japan is such a case.
China builds up for its own protection, Japan fears attack, and Japan builds up in answer.

waypoints.point: The same arms buildup is feared in one situation and not feared in another, so the security dilemma splits into cases where the dilemma arises easily and cases where the dilemma does not, and the split matters for understanding where the strongest power stands in the world: two large powers sit where the dilemma arises easily, while the strongest power sits where the dilemma does not.
waypoints.next_point: Two factors, offense-defense advantage and offense-defense distinguishability, are mainly what decides how readily the security dilemma arises.

cut the assertion of importance and move straight to the contrast — the reader has no reason to hold the two positions together and reads them as separate reports

paragraph_waypoints.point: The security dilemma — the trap in which one state's build-up for its own protection makes a neighbour fear attack and build up in turn — splits into cases where the dilemma arises easily and cases where it does not.
The same arms buildup is feared in one situation and not feared in another.
The split matters for understanding where the strongest power stands in the world.
Two large powers sit where the dilemma arises easily, while the strongest power sits where the dilemma does not.

waypoints.point: Two factors, offense-defense advantage and offense-defense distinguishability, are mainly what decides how readily the security dilemma arises.
